nodes.summary: For a sequence $x_0, x_1, \dots$ of keys and $m \ge 0$, the access frequency $q(i)$ of a key $i$ is the number of indices $j < m$ with $x_j = i$.
nodes.title: Access frequency

nodes.summary: For every assignment of positive weights $w$ to the keys, every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$ (no search-tree ordering is assumed), where $S_x$ is the splay operation, $\Phi_w$ the weighted potential, the cost is the number of rotations, or one if none, $W$ the weight and $f = \mathrm{focus}(x, t)$ the subtree at the end of the search path. With $r = \log_2 W$: the amortized time to splay a tree with root $t$…
nodes.title: Access lemma for splay trees

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$ (no search-tree ordering is assumed), where $S_x$ is the splay operation, $\Phi$ the potential, the cost is the number of rotations, or one if none, $|\cdot|$ counts nodes and $f = \mathrm{focus}(x, t)$ is the subtree at the end of the search path. It is the access lemma with every weight equal to one.
nodes.title: Access lemma for splay trees (unit weights)

nodes.summary: Let $w$ be positive item weights, $t$ a binary search tree of total weight $W$ and $x_0, \dots, x_{m-1}$ keys of $t$. Splaying successively at $x_0, \dots, x_{m-1}$, starting from $t$, costs in total at most Each access has amortized cost at most $3 \log_2 (W / w(x_j)) + 1$, and over the sequence the potential drops by at most $\sum_i \log_2 (W / w(i))$, because the subtree at the node holding $i$ always has weight…
nodes.title: Splay-tree access bound for arbitrary weights

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the tree component of the access of $x$ in $t$ is the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$.
nodes.title: The tree returned by a splay-tree access

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the access of $x$ in $t$ is the pair $(b, t')$, where $t'$ is the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ and $b$ is true exactly when $t'$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree access

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be an ordered binary tree over a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. When $t$ is split at $x$, every key of the left part is strictly less than $x$ and every key of the right part is strictly greater than $x$.
nodes.title: Splitting an ordered tree separates the keys around the split key

nodes.summary: For positive weights $w$ and a binary search tree $t$ containing the key $x$, that is, $O(\log(s(t)/s(x)))$ in Sleator and Tarjan's notation: in a search tree the search for $x$ ends at the node holding $x$, whose subtree has weight at least $w(x)$.
nodes.title: Amortized cost of accessing a present key

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$ with $n$ nodes, This is the access lemma with the term $-3\log_2 |\mathrm{focus}(x, t)|$ dropped, since that subtree has at least one node when $t$ is nonempty (and the bound reads $1 \le 1$ for the empty tree).
nodes.title: Amortized cost of a splay is at most `3 log₂ n + 1`

Then where the cost of a splay is its number of rotations, or one if it performs none. This is the explicit form of Sleator and Tarjan's Theorem 1: the total access time of $m$ accesses on an $n$-node splay tree is…
nodes.title: Balance theorem for splay trees

nodes.summary: For an ordered binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type and a key $x$, the splay-tree membership test of $x$ in $t$ returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Correctness of the splay-tree membership test

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the membership test of $x$ in $t$ is the Boolean component of the access of $x$ in $t$: it is true exactly when the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree membership test

nodes.summary: The cost of splaying $t$ at $x$ is $\max(1, \mathrm{rotations}(x, t))$: the number of rotations performed, or one if there are none. This is the measure of running time that Sleator and Tarjan use for splaying; it is proportional to the depth of the node splayed, and hence to the time of the search that precedes it.
nodes.title: Cost of a splay

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a binary search tree containing the key $x$, the [subtree at the end of the search path](focus.md) $\mathrm{focus}(x, t)$ is rooted at a node holding $x$. So in the [access lemma](access-lemma-weighted.md) the size $W(\mathrm{focus}(x, t))$ is the size $s(x)$ of the node holding $x$, which is at least $w(x)$.
nodes.title: In a search tree the search for a present key ends at its node

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$, `focus x t` is the subtree of $t$ rooted at the last node visited by the binary-search descent for $x$: the node holding $x$ if $x$ is present, and otherwise the node at which the search leaves the tree through an empty child. This is the node that the splay operation brings to the root, and $|\mathrm{focus}(x, t)|$ is the size $s(x)$ in the access lemma. The empty tree has…
nodes.title: Subtree at the end of the search path

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ equals the inorder traversal of $t$. No search-tree ordering of $t$ is assumed.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the inorder traversal

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, inserting $x$ into $t$ splays $x$ in $t$, splits the resulting tree at $x$ into a left part and a right part, and returns the tree whose root key is $x$, whose left subtree is the left part and whose right subtree is the right part.
nodes.title: Splay-tree insertion

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Keys after splay-tree insertion

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, if $y$ is a key of the left part or of the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$, then $y$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree split parts contain only original keys

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ and a binary tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ if and only if $y$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves membership

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs as a key of $t$, then $y$ occurs as a key of the left part or of the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$. The tree $t$ need not be a binary search tree.
nodes.title: Keys other than the split key survive a split

nodes.summary: Every tree `splayRun xs t i` has as many nodes as `t`.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the number of nodes along a run

nodes.summary: For every binary tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $x$, the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ has the same number of nodes as $t$.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the number of nodes

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ is again a binary search tree.
nodes.title: Splay-tree insertion preserves the search-tree property

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is again a binary search tree.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the search-tree property

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys in a linearly ordered type and let $x$ be a key. If $t$ is a binary search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), then the left part and the right part of the split of $t$ at $x$ are both binary search trees.
nodes.title: Both parts of a split search tree are search trees

nodes.summary: With every weight equal to one, the weighted potential of a binary tree equals its splay-tree potential: $\Phi_1(t) = \Phi(t)$. This is how the [unit-weight access lemma](access-lemma.md) is obtained from the access lemma.
nodes.title: Unit-weight potential is the splay-tree potential

nodes.summary: A binary tree with $n$ nodes has potential at most $n \log_2 n$: each of its $n$ subtrees has at most $n$ nodes. Together with the [nonnegativity of the potential](potential-nonneg.md), it bounds the net potential drop over any sequence of splays by $n \log_2 n$.
nodes.title: Upper bound on the splay-tree potential

nodes.summary: For every binary tree $t$, $\Phi(t) \ge 0$: each term of the potential is $\log_2$ of a subtree size, which is at least one.
nodes.title: The splay-tree potential is nonnegative

nodes.summary: For positive item weights $w$, the potential of a binary tree $t$ is the sum over the nodes $x$ of the rank $r(x) = \log_2 s(x)$, where $s(x) = W(t_x)$ is the weight of the subtree rooted at $x$. With unit weights it is the [splay-tree potential](potential.md).
nodes.title: Weighted splay-tree potential

nodes.summary: For a binary tree $t$, write $|u|$ for the number of nodes of a subtree $u$. The potential of $t$ is the sum over the nodes $x$ of $t$ of the rank $\log_2 |t_x|$ of the subtree $t_x$ rooted at $x$. This is Sleator and Tarjan's potential with every item of weight one, so that the size $s(x)$ of a node is the number of nodes below it.
nodes.title: Splay-tree potential

nodes.summary: For every binary tree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type and every key $x$, the splay-tree insertion of $x$ into $t$ is a nonempty tree whose root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Splay-tree insertion puts the inserted key at the root

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in a linearly ordered type (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), and let $x$ be a key that occurs in $t$. Then the tree obtained by splaying $x$ in $t$ is nonempty and its root key is $x$.
nodes.title: Root key after splaying a present key

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary search tree with keys in a linearly ordered type (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key of the node), and let $x$ be a key that occurs in $t$. Then there are binary trees $l$ and $r$ such that splaying $x$ in $t$ gives the tree whose root holds $x$, with left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$.
nodes.title: Splaying a present key brings it to the root

nodes.summary: The optional root key of a binary tree is undefined (none) for the empty tree, and is the key $k$ for a tree whose root node holds $k$.
nodes.title: Root key of a splay tree

nodes.summary: `rotations x t` is the number of single rotations performed by the [splay operation](splay.md) $S_x(t)$: zero when the root holds $x$ or the search stops at the root, one for a zig (including the fallback zig when the splayed grandchild subtree is empty), and two plus the rotations of the recursive call for a zig-zig or a zig-zag step.
nodes.title: Number of rotations performed by splaying

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, splaying $x$ in the empty binary tree gives the empty tree.
nodes.title: Splaying the empty tree

nodes.summary: For keys $x_0, x_1, \dots$ and a binary tree $t$, `splayRun xs t i` is the tree obtained from $t$ by splaying successively at $x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{i-1}$: it is $t$ for $i = 0$, and $S_{x_i}$ applied to the $i$-th tree otherwise.
nodes.title: Trees of a run of splays

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and write $(k; L, R)$ for the binary tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. For $x \in \alpha$, the splay $S_x(t)$ of a binary tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The empty tree splays to itself, and $t = (k; L, R)$ is left unchanged if $x = k$, if $x < k$ and $L$ is empty, or if $x > k$ and $R$ is empty. If $x < k$ and…
nodes.title: Splay operation

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $x \in \alpha$, and write $(k; L, R)$ for the binary tree with root key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. The split of a binary tree with keys in $\alpha$ at $x$ is the pair of trees defined by recursion: the empty tree splits into two empty trees; if $x < k$ and $L$ splits into $(L_1, L_2)$, then $(k; L, R)$ splits into $(L_1, (k; L_2, R))$; if $k < x$ and…
nodes.title: Search-path split at a key

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary search tree and $x_0, \dots, x_{m-1}$ keys of $t$ in which every key $i$ of $t$ occurs $q(i) \ge 1$ times. Splaying successively at $x_0, \dots, x_{m-1}$, starting from $t$, costs in total at most which is $O\bigl(m + \sum_i q(i) \log (m / q(i))\bigr)$ (the last sum is at most the middle one since $1 \le q(i) \le m$). In Sleator and Tarjan's words, for sufficiently long access sequences splay…
nodes.title: Static optimality of splay trees

nodes.summary: With every weight equal to one, the weight of a binary tree is its number of nodes: $W(t) = |t|$. So with unit weights the size $s(x)$ of a node is the number of nodes of its subtree, as in the unit-weight statements of this topic.
nodes.title: Unit weights give the number of nodes

nodes.summary: For every weight function $w$, key $x$ and binary tree $t$, the splayed tree $S_x(t)$ has the same weight as $t$: $W(S_x(t)) = W(t)$. Splaying preserves the inorder sequence of keys, and the weight is the sum of $w$ over that sequence. In the amortized analysis this keeps the total weight $W$ fixed along a sequence of splays.
nodes.title: Splaying preserves the weight of a tree

nodes.summary: For a weight function $w$ on keys, the weight $W(t)$ of a binary tree $t$ is the sum of $w(k)$ over the keys $k$ stored in its nodes; for $w = 1$ it is the number of nodes. With positive weights, the weight of the subtree rooted at a node $x$ is Sleator and Tarjan's size $s(x)$.
nodes.title: Weight of a binary tree

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
